title: Daily Health Briefing
intro: Good morning! Here's today's digest across your tracked topics — anti-aging, HIIT for women, pelvic floor training, integrative options for HER2+/TP53 breast cancer, and sleep. Each section distills recent, reputable findings from Nature, Frontiers, PubMed, ClinicalTrials.gov, JAMA Network, and the AASM, with citation chips below. Informational only — talk with a clinician about anything you'd act on.

sections.body:
This week's theme: the freshest **human** data is on **mitophagy** (urolithin A), while NAD-boosters like **NMN** stay in "modest and preliminary" territory.

- **Urolithin A & the aging immune system.** A 2025 *Nature Aging* randomized, placebo-controlled trial (50 healthy middle-aged adults, 1,000 mg/day for 4 weeks) found UA expanded **naive-like, less-exhausted CD8+ T cells** and improved immune-cell function — an early signal it may counter "inflammaging." Small and short, so think *promising*, not *proven*.
- **Reality check on the muscle claims.** A 2026 *Frontiers in Nutrition* systematic review (5 RCTs, 236 people) could only pool the 6-minute-walk test and found **no statistically significant benefit** (low certainty); strength/endurance signals were mixed. Expect subtle effects.
- **NMN.** A 2024 RCT (250 mg/day, 12 weeks, 60 older adults) raised blood **NAD+**, helped **maintain walking speed**, and modestly **improved sleep quality** vs. placebo — again, secondary outcomes.

Practical framing: favor ingredients with human RCTs, expect **modest** gains, and be wary of single-supplement "longevity" promises.

sections.body:
New 2026 evidence keeps HIIT a **time-efficient** way to build cardio fitness for women — with a clear reminder to **pair it with strength work**.

- **Middle-aged & older women.** A 2026 *Frontiers in Physiology* systematic review and meta-analysis (19 RCTs) found HIIT produced a **large, high-certainty improvement in VO2max** (SMD 1.20), consistent across ages and body types. But it showed **limited effect on muscle strength and physical function** — so HIIT alone isn't enough for overall fitness. Add resistance training.
- **Heart benefits.** A 2026 *International Journal of Obesity* RCT of young women with obesity (8 weeks, classic **4×4-minute** intervals at 85–95% max heart rate) found HIIT improved **myocardial efficiency** (work efficiency, reduced wasted work) more than moderate continuous training.

Practical takeaway: **~3 sessions/week**, intervals hard enough to feel breathless, progress volume gradually, keep recovery adequate — and layer in strength days for the results HIIT doesn't cover.

sections.body:
**Pelvic floor muscle training (PFMT)** remains the evidence-based, **first-line** treatment for stress urinary incontinence (SUI). Three fresh 2026 trials show how much it can do.

- **It can even delay surgery.** A 2026 *International Urogynecology Journal* RCT (90 women awaiting sling surgery) found **6 weeks of intensive PFMT** significantly improved muscle strength and symptom severity — and **43% postponed their planned operation** afterward.
- **A boost for very weak muscles.** A 2026 multicenter RCT found that adding **sEMG-triggered electrical stimulation** to supervised PFMT produced **earlier, greater, and longer-lasting** gains (sustained at 12 months) in women whose pelvic floors were too weak to train effectively alone.
- **Prevention in pregnancy.** A large 2026 *JAMA Network Open* RCT (764 first-time mothers) found an antenatal pelvic-floor workout **cut postpartum SUI** at 6 weeks (8.7% vs 13.9%).

Key point: **correct technique and consistency beat sheer reps.** Confirm you're activating the right muscles (a clinician or biofeedback helps); supervised programs generally outperform going it alone.

sections.topic: Alternative & Integrative Options — HER2+ / TP53 Breast Cancer
sections.body:
"Alternative" is best read as **evidence-based care used alongside standard treatment**, not instead of it. This week the most notable science is about **why TP53/p53 status matters** for HER2 disease.

- **A genetics-guided drug strategy.** A 2025 preclinical study (mouse models + organoids) showed that **HER2; TP53 co-mutated** tumors resist the pill **neratinib** but stay **sensitive to trastuzumab deruxtecan (T-DXd)** — because the p53 mutation opens up chromatin (more histone acetylation), making cells vulnerable to T-DXd's topoisomerase-I payload. **Neratinib + T-DXd** was highly effective together in the lab.
- **In the clinic.** That combination is being tested in an early-phase trial (**NCT05372614**) in HER2-altered solid tumors, with some early responses reported (note: the trial is currently listed as **suspended** for correlative sample analysis).

Important framing: this is **preclinical/early** evidence about *standard* targeted drugs — not a supplement or a substitute for HER2-directed therapy. Use it as a conversation-starter with your oncology team, especially if a TP53 mutation is known.

sections.body:
For chronic, restless, or disjointed sleep, 2026 guidance still puts **behavioral therapy ahead of pills and supplements**.

- **CBT-I stays first-line.** A new (April 2026) **AASM** clinical practice guideline on *combination* therapy issued two conditional recommendations: CBT-I **plus** medication beats **medication alone**, but combination is **not** better than **CBT-I alone** — because CBT-I often delivers durable improvement without drug risks.
- **Supplements, honestly.** AASM guidance has conditionally recommended **against** melatonin for chronic adult insomnia; it's most useful for **circadian** problems (jet lag, shift work). Evidence for **magnesium** in insomnia remains thin.
- **If sleep is genuinely "restless."** When there's an urge to move the legs, evening worsening, or relief with movement, screen for **restless legs syndrome**: AASM advises checking **iron studies (ferritin, transferrin saturation)** and treating low iron (e.g., ferritin ≤ 75 ng/mL).

Best-practice habits: keep a **fixed wake time**, reserve the bed **for sleep only**, keep the room cool/dark/quiet, wind down away from screens, and if disrupted sleep persists, see a provider to rule out **sleep apnea** and consider **CBT-I**.
